Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failure stems from ExtendedMessageFormat inheriting equals(Object) and hashCode() from java.text.MessageFormat while adding new state (notably, the registry of custom FormatFactory instances) and maintaining its own notion of the original pattern.

Evidence and how it leads to the failure:
- Test intent (org.apache.commons.lang3.text.ExtendedMessageFormatTest.testEqualsHashcode):
  - It constructs two ExtendedMessageFormat instances with the same pattern but different registries (LowerCaseFormatFactory vs UpperCaseFormatFactory).
  - It expects those instances to be considered different in identity and hashing, specifically asserting that their hash codes must differ: assertFalse("registry, hashcode()", emf.hashCode() == other.hashCode()) at line 301.
  - The test also explores “Different Class” and “Different pattern” scenarios, implying equals/hashCode must reflect subclass identity and original pattern content.

- Class state added by ExtendedMessageFormat:
  - A new field registry is introduced: private final Map<String, ? extends FormatFactory> registry; (line 82).
  - The constructor stores the registry and calls applyPattern: ExtendedMessageFormat(String pattern, Locale locale, Map<String, ? extends FormatFactory> registry) sets this.registry = registry and applyPattern(pattern) (lines 124–129).

- Pattern handling in applyPattern:
  - applyPattern(String pattern) parses the pattern with awareness of the registry to locate custom formats and builds two strings:
    - A “stripped” pattern (stripCustom) passed to super.applyPattern(...) (line 194).
    - A formatted pattern with custom descriptions reinserted (toPattern) maintained only inside ExtendedMessageFormat (line 195).
  - Crucially, when a custom format is recognized (format != null), the code avoids appending the custom format descriptor to the stripped pattern passed to the superclass (lines 170–179). This means the MessageFormat state will not reflect the presence of the custom format text when it is recognized via the registry.

- Root cause: equals/hashCode do not consider ExtendedMessageFormat’s added state.
  - ExtendedMessageFormat does not override equals(Object) or hashCode(), so it relies on MessageFormat’s implementations, which:
    - Do not know about ExtendedMessageFormat.registry.
    - Operate on the “stripped” pattern previously applied to the superclass (super.applyPattern(stripCustom.toString())) and thus may ignore the custom format descriptors entirely if they were recognized via the registry.
    - Do not enforce subclass identity (MessageFormat.equals typically uses instanceof MessageFormat), so instances of a subclass (e.g., OtherExtendedMessageFormat) can compare equal to ExtendedMessageFormat if the base state matches.
  - As a result, two ExtendedMessageFormat instances with the same base pattern and locale but different registries can end up with identical superclass-observed state (same stripped pattern, and MessageFormat-level state), producing identical hash codes. That violates the test’s expectation that different registries should yield different hash codes.

- Symptom in the failing test:
  - For “Different registry,” other is created with a different registry but same pattern and locale.
  - Since equals/hashCode are inherited and based on the superclass state (which excludes registry and custom format descriptors when recognized), emf.hashCode() == other.hashCode() can be true, making assertFalse(...) fail at line 301.

In summary, ExtendedMessageFormat adds meaningful state (registry and reconstructed toPattern) that affects formatting semantics, but it does not override equals(Object) and hashCode() to include that state and to respect subclass identity. This mismatch causes the hashCode collision (and potentially incorrect equals behavior) observed by the test.
